# Basic statistics

For a large majority of researchers, statistics is often reduced to selecting the correct statistical test and checking whether the resulting p-value meets the threshold for statistical significance. Under this mindset, an empirical study can feel fruitless if its results fail to achieve statistical significance.

Despite persistent efforts by statisticians to warn against the misuse of p-values and Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST), and despite the introduction of alternative metrics, standard testing practices remain deeply entrenched. This reductionist approach obscures the core philosophy of statistical thinking, fostering misunderstanding and, in some cases, methodological malpractice.

To build an intuitive understanding of statistics, the discipline can be divided into two main areas:

- Descriptive statistics, which focuses on defining populations, variables, probability distributions, and the numerical methods used to summarize data.
- Inferential statistics, which operates on the premise that collected data represents a sample of a broader population. Inferential methods provide rigorous tools to estimate true, unknown population parameters and quantify our uncertainty about those estimates.

This volume focuses primarily on descriptive statistics, while inferential statistics—which requires a deeper mathematical background—will be covered in a subsequent volume. Nevertheless, mathematical concepts and notation remain essential throughout this section. Readers seeking clarification on foundational notation are encouraged to review the preceding section on basic mathematics.

To touch on a familiar perspective, Mark Twain famously popularized the phrase: "There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics." This quote highlights how easily statistical presentation can be manipulated. On one end of the spectrum, individuals without statistical training may accept any presented number as absolute proof. On the other end, someone well-versed in statistics can intentionally transform data or cherry-pick tests to support a desired conclusion.

** Edit this: The goal of this section is to cultivate a deeper grasp of statistics, enabling researchers to gain genuine insights, make informed decisions, and think critically about data collection, sampling design, and analytical choices.
**
The section begins laying foundation for the statistical framework by defining a population (@sec-population) as the fundamental unit of study, and a variable (@sec-variable) as a function mapping a domain (the population) to a codomain (the observed values). From this perspective, the distinction between quantitative (@sec-quantitativeVariable) and qualitative (@sec-qualitativeVariable) variables depends directly on the mathematical properties of the codomain.

The remaining chapters cover data summarization:

- First-level description focuses on summarizing raw sequences of values through  distribution such as barchart and histogram (@sec-distribution) and cumulative distributions (@sec-cumulativeDist).
- Second-level description focuses on condensing distributions into single summary metrics. The Measures of central tendency  including the mean (@sec-mean), median (@sec-median), and mode (@sec-mode); and the measures of dispersion  including variance and standard deviation (@sec-variance), as well as quantiles (@sec-quantile).
